outline.target_audience: Undergraduate mathematics students or math enthusiasts

sections.title: Prerequisites: The Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)
sections.content: Briefly review the IVT: If a continuous function changes sign, it must cross zero. Visualize this as a hiker crossing a mountain range; if they start below a cloud layer and end above it, they must pass through the cloud.
sections.example: A hiker climbing from sea level to 1000m must pass through exactly 500m elevation.

sections.title: Problem Statement: The Inscribed Square
sections.content: Introduce the conjecture: Can every simple closed curve (a loop that doesn't intersect itself) have four points that form the vertices of a square? Show a circle and a random 'blob' shape side-by-side.
sections.example: Imagine a stretchy rubber band twisted into an irregular closed loop; we are searching for 4 points on that band that create a perfect square.

sections.title: Topological Mapping: The Configuration Space
sections.content: Explain how we map pairs of points $(x, y)$ on the curve to a 3D space. The set of all chords forms a surface. Explain that finding a square is equivalent to finding a point where the midpoint and distance conditions align.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'map' of all possible chords on the loop, where the axes represent the position of the two points on the boundary.

sections.title: The Solution Strategy: Parity and Symmetry
sections.content: Demonstrate the use of the 'winding number' or the antipodal map. If we rotate the square configuration, the difference between the 'midpoint' and the 'distance' constraints must vanish at some point due to continuous deformation.
sections.example: Using a robotic arm tracing the loop: as the arm adjusts to maintain a square, the continuous movement forces a intersection point where the 'square' property is satisfied.

sections.title: Summary and Open Frontiers
sections.content: Summarize that the theorem holds for all smooth curves (proven by Emch/Levien). Mention the generalization: the Inscribed Rectangle Problem (proven) vs. the Inscribed Square Problem for non-smooth curves (still an active area of research).
sections.example: Concluding with a digital animation of a square 'locking' into place on a dynamic, morphing organic shape.

storyboard.title: Prerequisites: The Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)
lecture_lines: Intermediate Value Theorem: Continuous functions crossing zero change sign.
Imagine a hiker crossing a mountain range.
If the hiker crosses, they must hit zero altitude.
animations: Display text: Intermediate Value Theorem on screen in #FFFFFF.
Draw a continuous function f(x) on a graph. Color #FFD700.
Highlight points a and b on the x-axis. Color #00FFFF.
Show f(a) < 0 and f(b) > 0 with labels. Color #FF4500.
Fade in a root point c where f(c)=0. Color #32CD32.

storyboard.title: Problem Statement: The Inscribed Square
lecture_lines: Can every closed loop contain an inscribed square?
Consider a circle or a complex blob.
We seek four points forming a square.
animations: Display title: The Inscribed Square Problem in #FFFFFF.
Show an arbitrary closed curve on a plane. Color #00CED1.
Attempt to fit a square within the curve. Color #FF6347.

storyboard.title: Topological Mapping: The Configuration Space
lecture_lines: We map curve point pairs to 3D space.
A surface represents all possible chords.
Midpoint and distance conditions reveal the square.
animations: Display title: Configuration Space in #FFFFFF.
Show a parameter space (s, theta) for the square. Color #9370DB.
Map the square vertices to the curve points. Color #FFA500.
Define a continuous function F on this space. Color #20B2AA.
Visualize the boundary of the configuration space. Color #FFD700.

storyboard.title: The Solution Strategy: Parity and Symmetry
lecture_lines: Parity and symmetry define our strategy.
We track square configurations along the loop.
Constraints vanish, forcing the square into existence.
animations: Display title: Symmetry and Parity in #FFFFFF.
Define f(s, theta) related to square side lengths. Color #FF6347.
Show the anti-symmetry of the function F. Color #32CD32.
Apply Borsuk-Ulam theorem to find a root. Color #FFD700.
Highlight the resulting inscribed square in the curve. Color #00FFFF.

storyboard.title: Summary and Open Frontiers
lecture_lines: The theorem holds for all smooth curves.
We explore rectangles and non-smooth loops.
The mystery of inscribed squares continues today.
animations: Display title: Summary: Square Inscribed in Curve in #FFFFFF.
Show the core result: a square always exists. Color #32CD32.
Briefly mention generalizations to other shapes. Color #FFD700.
